You've seen enough GRWM videos to know that plenty of people are incorporating lymphatic drainage tools into their morning routines. If you also grapple with regular facial puffiness, it's fair to wonder if lymphatic drainage tools could help.

These tools are marketed to encourage the flow of lymph, which is a clear, watery fluid that supports fluid balance and immune defenses in your body. The idea with lymphatic drainage tools—which include gua sha stones, facial rollers, dry brushes, and more—is to mechanically encourage the movement of lymphatic fluid to reduce puffiness and fluid retention.

Sources indicate that dermatologists say there's something to this. "Your lymph system helps move excess waste and fluid throughout the body," explains Joshua Zeichner, MD, director of cosmetic and clinical research at Mount Sinai Hospital. "Lymphatic massages help enhance activity of the system to circulate excess fluid and depuff.".

Industry observers note that doctors may recommend lymphatic drainage massage to people with health conditions like lymphedema or to post-surgical patients, indicates Ife J. Rodney, MD, founding director of Eternal Dermatology + Aesthetics. For everyone else, the data is less clear on whether lymphatic drainage offers much benefit.

Industry observers note that "For everyday facial puffiness, gentle massage may offer temporary improvement, though research on gua sha is limited," Dr. Rodney claims. Note the "temporary" part of what she said. Despite what you may hear on social media, lymphatic drainage won't permanently alter your cheekbones and jawline, although Dr. Rodney says this may help your skin look fresher and your features look more defined. "Think of it as an optional self-care step, not a requirement for healthy skin," Dr. Rodney says.

Industry observers note that want to opt into this? There is a range of tools to consider—and doctors say you don't need to spend a ton to get results.

It has been revealed that A gua sha tool needs to have at least one smooth edge for lymphatic drainage. But Face Gym's Multi-Sculpt High-Performance Contouring Tool has six different edges to focus on different areas of your face. Long and medium smooth edges are made for classic lymphatic drainage, while shorter sides are ideal for areas around your eyes. The tool even includes rounded teeth for fine lines and a targeted tip for acupressure. (Face Gym has an instructional video to help guide you through all of this.).

In a recent development, face Gym's gua sha tool is made from stainless steel, which is hypoallergenic and easy to clean. The stainless-steel tool is easy to clean, but any product can irritate skin. It also has a nice cooling effect after briefly popping it into the fridge. While this gua sha tool is on the pricier end, its stainless steel construction means it won't shatter like its crystal counterparts if you accidentally drop it.

Sources indicate that both are used for facial massage, but a roller moves across the skin by rolling, while gua sha uses sweeping strokes with a smooth-edged tool. You simply glide the roller across your face with gentle pressure to support lymphatic drainage. This is another stainless steel tool, which means it's a little more hygienic and easy to clean than its more traditional crystal versions. It's also highly likely to survive in the event of a drop.

The stainless steel has a natural cooling feel against the skin, although you can toss it in the fridge for extra chilliness. This tool is heavier than stone or crystal rollers—keep that on the back burner if you're used to those. It also pairs best with an oil or serum to help it glide smoothly over your skin, so plan to moisturize at the same time.

It has been revealed that dry brushing has the combined benefit of supporting lymphatic drainage and exfoliation at once. But some brushes have stiff bristles that can feel intense—and even irritating—against the skin. Esker's dry brush is gentle against the skin, but still feels firm enough to get things moving.

Esker's dry brush has a spa-like feel, along with an ergonomic design that's easy to grip. It's relatively petite, too, making it easy to toss in a bag for travel or trips to the gym. The only downside of that is the handle isn't long enough to reach your back. (That's more of an exfoliation glitch vs. a lymphatic drainage problem, though.) The rules of lymphatic drainage still apply with a brush like this—if it feels irritating to your skin, stop. But if dry brushing is something you're into and you want to try lymphatic drainage on areas of your body other than your face, this is a solid choice.

Sources indicate that most people do gua sha on their face with a sculpting stone, crystal, or steel device. But not everyone is into the sensation of moving something hard across the sensitive skin in that area. Skin Gym answers the call with a face brush designed specifically for gua sha.

The brush is densely packed with soft bristles, creating a feel like you're swiping a really good makeup brush over your skin. It has an ergonomic shape, making it easy to glide over the contours of your face. This brush is pretty beginner-friendly, making it a good entry point if you're gua sha-curious. But be aware that you may not be able to get as much pressure on your skin (if that's even your thing) as you would with a stone or other hard tool. The brush also requires regular cleaning to avoid pushing dirt around your face.

In a recent development, let's get this out of the way upfront: Vibration plates are a controversial tool. Many make bold claims, like that they can support weight loss or mimic the effects of exercise—those are unfounded. But these plates can improve circulation and lymphatic drainage as a result, as Rachelle Reed, PhD, an exercise scientist based in Athens, Georgia, previously told Women's Health.

Industry observers note that FWIW, research suggests that you'll get many of the same circulation- (and lymph-)promoting effects from exercise. But if a vibrating plate is more your speed, the LifePro Waver is worth a look. This machine offers 99 speed levels to allow you to fine-tune the intensity. The motor is also quiet, so you don't have to stress about waking up other people in your home. This plate comes with resistance bands and free online workout videos, too. Just be aware that vibration plates aren't safe for everyone—you should take a pass if you're pregnant, prone to blood clots, or struggle with dizziness, for example. Bachelorette star Gabby Windey also recently shared that she broke her back after cranking up her (unnamed) vibrating plate in the name of lymphatic drainage. Though her account is an individual anecdote and doesn’t establish the typical risk, proceed with caution. But if you're looking for a way to get lymphatic drainage moving around your whole body, this is worth considering.

The best type of lymphatic drainage tool for you depends on where you proposal to use it on your body. "These types of massages can be performed anywhere, but are extremely common on the face," Dr. Zeichner claims. "Oftentimes, a smooth, but firm tool like gua sha is used.".

According to recent reports, A roller is another option for facial lymphatic drainage, and is usually considered more gentle than gua sha. For lymphatic drainage other than the face, some people reach for dry brushes and vibration plates.

For gua sha, Dr. Rodney suggests choosing a tool with smooth, rounded edges with no sharp spots, chips, or cracks. "It should be comfortable to hold and easy to clean," she claims—and that applies to all lymphatic drainage tools. For gua sha and rollers, "you don't need an expensive crystal," Dr. Rodney says.

Dry brushes should also have natural fibers, since synthetic can feel harsh against the skin. Overall, "a smooth finish and gentle technique matter more than the price tag," Dr. Rodney states.

Sources indicate that there's no exact weight for a lymphatic drainage tool that's best for everyone. Instead, it should feel substantial in your hand—but not too heavy or too light. You want to be able to comfortably use your tool, and allow the tool to apply pressure vs. heavy force from you.

They may temporarily reduce puffiness for some people, but evidence for at-home tools and broader health benefits is limited. "For everyday facial puffiness, gentle massage may offer temporary improvement," Dr. Rodney indicates. Dr. Zeichner agrees. "Especially if you wake up puffy in the morning after drinking too much alcohol, not having enough sleep, taking in too much salt, or during your menstrual cycle, lymphatic massages can be a useful tool," he says. Just keep in mind that the effects are temporary.

Recent findings suggest that every type of tool is slightly different. "The goal of a lymphatic massage is to improve the body's drainage system," Dr. Zeichner says. "That is why the massage should be performed in a particular way." If you're massaging your face, the pressure should start near the center of your face, before moving out and down toward your collarbones. This follows the natural lymphatic flow, Dr. Zeichner says.

According to recent reports, "A few minutes is enough to start," Dr. Rodney notes. "Keep the pressure light—bruising is a sign to stop, not a sign it’s working.".

Dermatologists recommend taking a pass on lymphatic drainage tools if your skin is irritated, infected, sunburned, or broken. (That includes inflamed acne, eczema, or rosacea flares, per Dr. Rodney.).

According to recent reports, dr. Rodney also suggests checking with your doctor if you take blood thinners, bruise easily, or have blood clots, heart or kidney failure, lymphedema, or a history of cancer treatment or lymph node removal. "After cosmetic procedures or surgery, get clearance from your treating clinician," she says. "Persistent or painful swelling needs an explanation before it needs a massage.".

Sources indicate that skip the cotton—it’s a sweat sponge. Synthetic fabrics like polyester blends are moisture-wicking and dry quickly, while nylon blends are more breathable for hot weather. Bonus: Some materials, like merino wool, are naturally anti-stink, while others feature built-in odor-fighting technology to keep you smelling fresh, no matter how hard you go.

Lined shorts offer built-in support, making them ideal for high-impact activities. If you’re lifting heavy or going ape on the air bike, the liner is a win. For casual workouts or layering over tights, unlined shorts let you move freely and stay cool.

The inseam is the length of the shorts from your nether region to the inside hem, and getting it right can make or break your workout. If you’re doing moves like squats, lunges, or anything that’s got you moving deep and low, shorter inseams (think 5 to 7 inches) are your best bet for keeping things smooth and unrestricted. While shorter inseams offer better mobility, longer inseams of 9 to 11 inches are great for taller athletes or anyone who wants extra coverage. Just keep in mind, if you’re on the shorter side, too much fabric can feel bulky and might even slow you down.

Functional storage is a must. "I say pockets are a must for me, and an extra bonus if they zip. Not a pocket in the back of my waist that I can barely reach, but pockets on the front sides," states Andy Stern from Rumble Boxing. Side pockets keep your essentials handy, and zippers keep you from chasing keys mid-jog.

Industry observers note that your gym shorts should feel as good as they look. Gym shorts should fit snugly around your waist—no squeezing, no sliding down mid-squat. Think "secure but free to move," like your gym buddy who knows when to spot you and when to back off. If you’re lunging and your shorts are riding up, it’s time to re-evaluate.

When it comes to picking gym shorts, it’s all about matching your moves. If you’re running, go for shorter inseams and split hems—you want freedom of movement, not fabric flapping around like you’re in a wind tunnel. Plus, reflective details keep you visible, because dodging traffic shouldn’t be part of your cardio. For lifting, you’ll need durable fabrics and compression liners to keep everything secure while you chase your personal best—nobody needs a wardrobe malfunction mid-squat. And for yoga? Think soft, stretchy, and unlined, so you can nail that downward dog without feeling like your shorts are plotting against you.

Flattering shorts come down to fit, proportion, and the right inseam for your build. If you’ve got beefy legs, short shorts will always work in your favor. Show them off with a 5-inch inseam (or less), which hits mid-thigh for most guys. For a touch more coverage, go with a 7-inch inseam, the most popular length for a casual, everyday look. Aim for a slight taper through the leg so it holds its shape without clinging. Bonus points for a smooth waistband that won’t dig in.

#64208. Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1036 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.
  • The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also shows that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.
  • These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.

The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also shows that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.

These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.

In a recent development, this is significant given that autoimmune diseases, conditions in which the body’s immune system attacks its own healthy cells, are estimated to affect around 4.6% of the U.S. population. Additionally, despite the observed disparities in diagnoses, women are almost two times as likely as men to be diagnosed with an autoimmune disease.

Researchers conducted an online survey between December 7, 2024, and March 7, 2025, inviting adults ages 18 and older who had a confirmed autoimmune or rheumatic disease.

The survey was carefully designed and tested with input from patients, charities, and medical experts to ensure it captured important information about patients’ diagnostic journeys.

Participants were asked about the time it took from when they first noticed symptoms to when they received their autoimmune diagnosis.

They also reported how many healthcare visits they made before diagnosis and whether they felt their symptoms were ever misdiagnosed as mental health issues, psychosomatic problems (physical symptoms caused or worsened by psychological factors), or another physical disease.

The survey was widely shared on social media, patient support groups, and community organizations to reach a broad audience.

Special efforts were made to include underrepresented groups such as males, younger individuals, and people from minority ethnic backgrounds.

The survey was available in five languages, and participants could complete it with help from researchers if needed.

To analyze the data, the team used statistical methods, adjusting for factors like age, type of autoimmune disease, continent of residence, and financial situation.

These methods helped compare the experiences of males and females while accounting for differences in disease types and other factors.

It has been revealed that the study included 6,607 participants, with 91.2% identifying as female and most living in the United Kingdom. On average, women were younger than men in the study.

In a recent development, autoimmune thyroid disease was the most common condition reported. Non-autoimmune conditions like anxiety were more commonly reported by women, while men reported higher rates of hypertension.

According to recent reports, one of the main findings was that women reported longer delays before getting a diagnosis. Nearly 32% of females experienced delays of four years or more from symptom onset to diagnosis, compared to about 26% of males.

On the other hand, men were more likely to be diagnosed within a year of symptom onset (nearly 50% of males versus 40% of females).

Women also made more visits to healthcare providers before diagnosis, with 26.2% having 11 or more visits compared to 18.4% of men.

When it came to misdiagnoses, women were significantly more likely to report that their symptoms had been mistaken for mental health challenges (43.3% of females vs. 32.7% of males) or psychosomatic causes (33.9% of females vs. 21.5% of males).

However, there was no significant difference between men and women in being misdiagnosed with another physical disease.

The type of autoimmune disease also influenced misdiagnosis rates. Diseases with clear physical symptoms or definitive lab tests, like type 1 diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, had lower rates of mental health and psychosomatic misdiagnoses.

In contrast, conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease had higher rates of these misdiagnoses (over 50%).

After adjusting for disease type and other factors, women still had higher odds of reporting mental health or psychosomatic misdiagnoses compared to men.

Other factors affected misdiagnosis rates, too. People living in continents outside the United Kingdom, those with lower household income, and certain disease groups were more likely to report psychiatric or psychosomatic misdiagnoses. Age, however, was not linked to the risk of being misdiagnosed.

According to recent reports, muhammad Qasim, MD, a pulmonologist and medical writer with MySleepApneaTeam, told Healthline that autoimmune diseases are often difficult to diagnose. Qasim wasn’t involved in the study.

It has been revealed that “Early symptoms can be vague, fluctuate over time, and affect several parts of the body,” he said. “Fatigue, pain, sleep problems, brain fog, and mood changes do not immediately point to one diagnosis.”.

Qasim echoed the study’s findings, explaining that similar symptoms may be interpreted differently in women versus men, with complaints being attributed to anxiety, stress, or psychosomatic causes.

However, there are probably multiple factors contributing to this phenomenon, he stated.

“Differences in disease presentation, gaps in research, fragmented care, and unconscious bias can all contribute,” noted Qasim. “Once a psychiatric explanation enters the medical record, there is also a risk that later clinicians view newly introduced symptoms through that same lens.”.

Regarding unconscious bias, the study’s authors noted that women have historically been treated by doctors as “less credible” and more “emotional” in reporting their symptoms, which can influence how doctors interpret them.

These disparities in diagnosis are key, however, because longer waits and erroneous diagnoses can delay proper treatment and increase women’s frustration, leading them to stop asking for help.

The researchers suggest that healthcare providers need to be aware of these concerns and consider autoimmune diseases carefully when patients, especially females, present with more complicated symptoms.

Adam Carewe, MD, a physician in Boulder, CO, and a clinical informaticist with General Medicine who wasn’t involved in the study, offered guidance to those experiencing symptoms on how to obtain a proper diagnosis.

It has been revealed that healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Patients can keep an accurate symptom timeline, bring in family history, ask what else could be explaining these symptoms, ask for a strategy for next steps if initial testing/treatment, do not change anything, and lastly get a second opinion,” he advised.

Carewe emphasized the value of not giving up on finding answers. “The most important thing for anyone with persistent symptoms of any kind is to continue to work with your primary care clinician and continue to advocate for yourself,” he said.

Industry News: Ivy Shapiro's Manhattan Home is an Artful Ode to Old-School New York

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Describing the allure of her sprawling prewar Manhattan apartment, art adviser Ivy Shapiro returns to one theme again and again.
  • Recent findings suggest that A Joel Shapiro sculpture holds a corner of the dining room beneath a painting by Aubrey Saget.
  • In a recent development, in the living room, a painting by Cecily Brown hangs above a Joel Shapiro table with sculptures by Jonathan Borofsky (left) and Ivy Shapiro’s daughter, Lily Crewdson (right), beside a Southeast Asian sculpture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Describing the allure of her sprawling prewar Manhattan apartment, art adviser Ivy Shapiro returns to one theme again and again. “It’s old-school,” she insists. “I have this fantasy that I’m living in a different era. I wanted the apartment to capture this nostalgic vision of old-school New York elegance.” She had plenty to work with. The bones of the unit—its high ceilings, architectural details, and idiosyncratic layout of generous salons and small, meandering rooms—remained largely intact. Major structural alterations were unnecessary to make the space her own, a home that reflects her singular character while graciously accommodating an extensive collection of art that ranges from Stone Age tools and Southeast Asian antiquities to modern and contemporary works created by friends and family.

Recent findings suggest that A Joel Shapiro sculpture holds a corner of the dining room beneath a painting by Aubrey Saget. Works on paper by Edgar Degas and Bob Thompson surmount the fireplace, which is clad in black encaustic tile by clé.

In a recent development, in the living room, a painting by Cecily Brown hangs above a Joel Shapiro table with sculptures by Jonathan Borofsky (left) and Ivy Shapiro’s daughter, Lily Crewdson (right), beside a Southeast Asian sculpture. A Jasper Johns lithograph hangs at rear. Sculpture in foreground by Tony Smith.

A Jeremy Anderson chandelier from Gallery Fumi crowns the makeup room. On the wall are works on paper by Cecily Brown.

In a recent development, shapiro was born into the Latest York art world of the 1970s, when the artist and collector community had a far different complexion than that of today, a time before “the art world” meant “the art-fair world.” She is the daughter of the late celebrated sculptor Joel Shapiro and art educator Amy Snider, and the stepdaughter of artist Ellen Phelan. Hers is a life organized around and by art, so it is no surprise that the same would be true of her apartment. Here, art is offered the same sovereignty as the home’s human inhabitants, the freedom to take up space, require concessions, demand attention, and even, occasionally, to trip you up. It doesn’t have to fit in above a sofa or over a mantel, nor does it have to stand for something—taste, wealth, a movement, a generation. She accords each piece the independence to exist on its own terms, to be at home.

According to recent reports, “I like hanging art in weird places where people don’t like to hang,” Shapiro claims. “It’s not an intellectual exercise. It’s more intuitive.”.

Architect Raffaella Bortoluzzi, Shapiro’s accomplice in the gentle transformation of the home, drew inspiration from her client’s unconventional sensibility. “I love that Ivy decided not to combine the small rooms and try to impose a more contemporary approach on how the spaces flow. We wanted to respect the historic character and maintain the eccentricities,” Bortoluzzi notes. “Our idea was that every room should have its own little story. We focused on light, playful treatments that in no way fight the original architecture.”.

Floating tiled shelves in the kitchen display ceramics by Warren MacKenzie and Shio Kusaka and a small sculpture by Joel Shapiro.

The television room features paintings by Lothar Hempel (left) and Elizabeth Murray (right).

A Joel Shapiro drawing has pride of place in the bedroom of Ivy Shapiro’s son, Walker Crewdson. To the right are a drawing by Sol LeWitt and a Joel Shapiro print.

The television room, for example, is enrobed in aubergine Venetian plaster. The home office, covered in a crimson plaster, features shelves and drawer fronts finished with a surface treatment of crushed eggshells encased in epoxy. Bortoluzzi goosed the primary bath by sprinkling a handful of Piero Fornasetti tiles among a field of pearlescent, zellige-like ones. In Shapiro’s makeup room, ladylike pink plaster walls are amplified by an antique mirror, custom shoe closets with floral fabric behind the glass case fronts, and a sprightly Jeremy Anderson chandelier. “Ivy is very funny and feminine in her way,” the architect states. “The design speaks to those aspects of her personality.”.

In the dining room, a Jean Arp collage is installed above an antique tansu with Stone Age tools and Joel Shapiro maquettes.

Recent findings suggest that the last sculpture Joel Shapiro created rests on a table in the primary bedroom. The painting is by Bob Thompson. The sofa is covered in a Rubelli brocade.

Shelves and drawer fronts in the home office are covered in a surface material of crushed eggshells by Nature Squared.

According to recent reports, within the newly refurbished architectural shell, Shapiro deployed her estimable collection of art and objets de vertu with wit and verve. In the living room, the way that Jonathan Borofsky’s bronze Split Head sculpture is balanced by the split-off stone head of an Asian deity feels like a call and response across the ages, as well as a vignette about the endurance of art. They flank a dynamic painting by Shapiro’s friend Cecily Brown like chaperones at an orgy of color and motion. A sculpture by Shapiro’s daughter, Lily Crewdson, joins the Borofsky piece atop a table made by her father, one of many Joel Shapiro sculptures, drawings, and maquettes installed throughout the apartment.

A sculpture by Richard Artschwager is installed above a Joel Shapiro bronze in a hallway.

An Axel Salto sculpture sits beneath an artwork by Ryan Sullivan in the living room.

In the hallway to the primary bedroom, a lyrical vintage Danish wall light of abstracted vines, leaves, and flowers hangs above a signature Carl Andre metal floor sculpture, the ultimate butch/femme pairing. In the bedroom itself, a sculpture that Joel Shapiro made in the hospital during his final days (he died in June of 2025) sits inconspicuously on a small table of his own design. It was the last artwork of his storied career.

“Living with so much of Joel’s art, and all these amazing things he and Ellen collected, connects me to [my dad],” Shapiro muses. “The way the apartment is set up, I feel like my life is completely integrated with the art.”.

  • Recent findings suggest that IN 2001, I was an obese drug addict.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that SEPTEMBER 2026, THE week of the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal and the city was lousy with bicycles. On most corners, a new pack of amateur cyclists gathered. Bixi—Montreal’s bike share program—was represented, but as a garnish to the inundation of mountain, beach, fixie, and road bikes, along with their riders from around the world, taking over the city. I watched all this in awe. Cycling changed me because it taught me how to suffer. The sport familiarized me with the type of suffering that wrecks you, but you put yourself through it on purpose. You suffer to emerge resilient and better.

I'd heard elite cyclists—guys like Toms Skujins, Sean Quinn, and Mike Woods—talk about this pain in passing, but I was in Montreal to learn more. I wanted to know if they saw the power of suffering in the same way I did.

Recent findings suggest that IN 2001, I was an obese drug addict. Checking into rehab that year put a number to my weight: 536 pounds. I’d been diagnosed with congestive heart failure, drugs were rapidly killing me, and I was motivated to change. Once I’d been sober for a year, I was able to see that my weight was causing me suffering.

In a recent development, standing was a herculean effort, placing my feet in the right spot to support me, calculating the angle my knees would be in at the apex of my shifting mass, deep breath, locked core, and a hope and a prayer that I didn’t topple. Tying my shoes was done in bursts of held breath and near-blackouts. I slept sitting up, because the pressure of my chest caused me to choke and gasp. I could once soothe that suffering with food and drugs and kick that discomfort down the road a bit, but in sobriety I needed healthy outlets.

I’d successfully managed lose 100 pounds before my wife tricked me into going to the gym. When she’d ask that I go, I’d tell her that the gym was a place for fit people. So she bought me a package with a personal trainer, said I could flake on the appointments, but I’d be flushing money down the toilet if I did. I went, but I was geared towards avoidance, and whenever something in the gym got hard, I’d just tell the trainer I couldn’t do it.

According to recent reports, riding a bike was something I did during outings with my wife and little kids maybe a few times a year. We’d cram our minivan full of bikes, find the flattest part of the Venice bike path, and slowly cruise for ten minutes at a time. Getting them back into the car was the hardest thing I had to work through.

Little did I know that someday cycling would be the key to changing my life.

ROUND AND ROUND I went losing and regaining weight. In 2009, after getting down to 300 pounds and ballooning back up to over 400, faced with having to start over once again, I turned my sights to running.

In a recent development, I tried running on a desolate stretch of the LA river near my house in Studio City. Not only was I unbearably slow, running hurt. My flat feet sent electric jolts of white-hot pain cascading up and through my body. That first day, I’d wrapped my ankles so tightly with ace bandages that my toes went numb. My feet were no better off and my nipples bled. The next day I could barely stand. The suffering didn’t stop when I stopped running. My feet, ankles, knees, and hips hurt long after—and I had no control over it.

In a recent development, with running out, but I turned to an old beach cruiser in our shed. The street we lived on was relatively flat, but every street branching off it was a steep climb. After a few rounds on my street, I decided to be ballsy and see how long I could last going uphill.

In a recent development, my legs were screaming, but there was no electric jolt of pain in my pedal stroke. My heart thundered, my mind told me I had to stop. But without the jarring jolt I got when my feet hit the ground while running, I knew I could go further.

Despite never riding my bike uphill as a kid, despite weighing 400 pounds, despite every physical and mental signal in me telling me to quit, I made it up to the top of that hill, up to Mulholland and Laurel Canyon, and it was glorious. Fighting through that urge to stop was incredible; getting to the top even more so. The pain while running was a warning that stayed with me after I stopped. The pain of cycling uphill was legs, lungs, and heart. I could push through it, and it stopped when I stopped.

In a recent development, I asked Tour de France cyclist Mike Woods about this distinction of suffering when I was in Montreal. “Suffering is a bit of a misnomer for endurance events. Are you really suffering? It’s elected, you know?” he told me. “You choose the pain, you choose when to stop, you choose when to keep going. I don’t truly suffer. Suffering is when you don’t choose for that pain to be inflicted on you”.

And then he remarked something that really resonated with me: “But it does prepare you for real suffering, when you have something bad happen to you in life. Doing endurance events, I find—it’s fake suffering, but when you have those bad moments in your life, you’re better prepared to manage them.”.

It has been revealed that AFTER THAT HILL climb, I started riding my bike regularly, eventually graduated to a mountain bike, and then to a road bike. I rode to the top of every mountain in Los Angeles. I discovered I was capable of so much more than my mind or body allowed me to believe. Legs screaming, heart pounding, mind numbing, this was suffering, and I found that I loved it. And, like Woods stated, I found that the more I suffered on a bicycle, the less I suffered off it.

Sources indicate that “One day at a time, one pedal stroke at a time. Just move forward,” Toms Skujins, a two-time Latvian road race champion, told me in Montreal. “When you’re racing, you can stop at any point. You’re the one doing the damage, you know? That’s very voluntary suffering, because there’s, obviously, things in the world that happen where you don’t choose to suffer, and you have no choice there. Here… if your legs are screaming too much, you can just stop. For me, that kind of suffering is definitely easier to take.”.

Sources indicate that within my first year of cycling, I was riding every day. There was a loop that took me from Studio City over the hill to West Hollywood. I’d cross Los Angeles, ride up PCH, cross the Santa Monica Mountains, and ride back to Studio City along Ventura Boulevard. It got me 100 miles and 8,000 feet of climbing, and I did it a few times a week. I’d do shorter 30- to 50-mile rides on the remaining days.

Sean Quinn, a US pro cyclist, gets it: “It sounds easy when you’re sitting on the couch, but when you’re actually in that moment suffering, your body’s basically sending you all the signals it can to make you just do anything else, just stop, stop the suffering,” he told me. “There’s no instant fix to a lot of your suffering. You have to be patient, accept that it’s gonna be shitty for a while, and wait it out, and keep a cool head, and eventually it does get better. Of course, you have to take action.”.

It has been revealed that when I was riding every day, I got down to 213 pounds. I’d like to say I stayed there. But I went back to work, stopped riding, my diet unraveled, and over the next few years, I gained nearly all of it back.

In 2016, 400 pounds again, I ruptured the biceps tendon in my right arm and had to have surgery to repair it. As a sober guy, I turned down the post-op painkillers. I was up all night in pain and had to work the following day. On set, with the motion of production buzzing around me, the pain was dull, but it was unrelenting, just like a ride up Angeles Crest Highway, more than 120 miles out-and-back, with over 13,000 feet of elevation gain. I hadn’t chosen the injury, but I had chosen to go without the pills, and that reminded me of the pain on the bike, something I picked and something I knew would come to an end. I’d remind myself of that and go back to learning my lines and preparing for the scene.

It has been revealed that that day reminded me that I knew how to do this. So I got back on a diet, and by 2018 I was down to 260, and I’ve held steady there ever since.

According to recent reports, riding a bike taught me that I could suffer now in benefit of tomorrow. It’s been the most powerful lesson I’ve learned about myself.

Sources indicate that ON THE DAY of the elite men’s road race, we fans lined the streets. There was dedicated bike parking near the finish line—Fans Village Bonjour Montreal—with thousands of bikes in neat rows. We all lined up to watch the attacks, riders going solo for that long and treacherous circuit. An American, Brandon McNulty, went off the front with about three laps to go and won the World Championship this year. It was thrilling to see. At the press conference afterward he mentioned, “I was just dying, but I kept pushing.”.

Leaving Canada, I couldn’t help but think that I shared something with everyone else there for the races. A secret membership, dues paid in sweat, and a code, to respect and revel in my voluntary suffering.

I’d gone to Montreal to ask the riders if they saw suffering the way I did, and in different words, all three told me that what you do on the bike carries over into the rest of your life. I’d thought cycling taught me how to suffer, but what it did was give me a place where I was in control of it, where I could make it a practice, so that when the suffering of life came along, the suffering I had no control over, I was better equipped to deal with it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its newly introduced NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

In a recent development, when the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The firm’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The upcoming NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

On top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

According to recent reports, power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

It has been revealed that why is this article written like it will be available in the US market? It’s made in China and has Chinese software, we’ll never see it.

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the latest NX7 in the comments, today.

#64196. Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

📅 17 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (758 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

📅 17 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (758 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.
  • This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.
  • In a recent development, it is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

In a recent development, it is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

It has been revealed that the researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

In a recent development, MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

It has been revealed that ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she stated.

It has been revealed that research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion remarked that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is vital for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she mentioned.

“These become particularly important at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:.

Industry observers note that “These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross remarked.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an key part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion said.

#64193. The Science Behind Mogging

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1516 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

The Science Behind Mogging

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AT SIX-FOOT-FOUR, I’m not accustomed to feeling physically dwarfed.
  • In a recent development, until recently, I didn’t have a name for this peculiar, perhaps Palaeolithic phenomenon.
  • Recent findings suggest that “To mog” entered the lexicon thanks to figures like Braden Peters, better known as Clavicular.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AT SIX-FOOT-FOUR, I’m not accustomed to feeling physically dwarfed. Sure, I might not have bulging muscles—but I confess I occasionally survey the other men in the gym and entertain the idea that I might be the hottest guy in the room. Sometimes, though, a bigger, better looking dude walks in and starts lifting heavier weights than me. My confidence evaporates, along with, I imagine, the admiring glances of all the men and women (who, on reflection, might not actually have been paying me any mind).

In a recent development, until recently, I didn’t have a name for this peculiar, perhaps Palaeolithic phenomenon. Mogging, derived from “alpha Male Of the Group,” describes the act of one man outshining another, through any combination of height, muscularity, facial attractiveness, status, or charisma (a.k.a. “aura”). On the receiving end, it’s the sudden, visceral realization that another man might be stronger or better-looking than you, and the cascade of feelings of inferiority that follow.

Recent findings suggest that “To mog” entered the lexicon thanks to figures like Braden Peters, better known as Clavicular. The 20-year-old looksmaxxing influencer was spectacularly “frame-mogged” on his own livestream in a viral moment earlier this year. The curious phrasing captured online attention, and on November 3 “mogging” was crowned Collins Dictionary’s word of the year for 2026.

It has been revealed that but this type of social scenario didn’t just emerge with the dawn of the internet. I was curious: Does this emasculating sensation stem from an ancient status instinct, an ego threat, a form of social comparison, or something else? And why are some men so sensitive to it?

THIS ISSUE OF mogging raises a question: Why should another man’s stature have such an immediate effect on my self-esteem? It’s a theme explored in the classics. In Homer’s Iliad, the ancient Greek epic, King Priam spots the enormous warrior Ajax, “whose head and shoulders tower above the rest.” Yet Homer also understood that size wasn't everything. Earlier in the same passage, Menelaus is described as broader-shouldered than Odysseus, the cunning hero played by Matt Damon in The Odyssey—but the shorter man’s extraordinary eloquence renders his stature irrelevant.

Sources indicate that modern researchers have also looked for answers. Human judgment “is by nature comparative” and social comparisons are “spontaneous, effortless, and unintentional reactions to the performance of others,” according to a 2014 review of the early indications on the brain mechanisms of social comparison and their influence on the reward system.

Meanwhile, other related research found that physically stronger men were perceived as having higher social status, partly because they were considered more capable leaders. But does this make the discomfort of being mogged inevitable?

Industry observers note that psychologists distinguish between dominance, in which status is secured through intimidation, and prestige, which is earned through the admiration of others. Research suggests that even if the strongest and most attractive may initially draw outsized attention, or mog, prestige is ultimately conferred upon those who benefit the group, rather than pursue aggressive self-interest.

Industry observers note that for couples therapist Sarah Tilley, this dynamic reflects the tension between our instinctive deference to appearances and our recognition of its limitations. Snap judgments of competence from candidates’ faces predicted almost 69 percent of US senate races in 2004, according to a study in Science,.

“There is a deference to beauty and we’re all culprits,” she says. “Beauty trumps intelligence, but only for a short amount of time. Smart people will know that, but it takes wisdom.” In other words, the actual effects of a mog could be fleeting if there is someone smarter in the room.

Industry observers note that WHAT IS ACTUALLY happening when you feel the mog? Turns out, there are chemical responses behind those feelings of self-doubt.

“A review of more than 200 lab studies found that our cortisol is reliably spiked when we feel that others are judging us and when we can’t control the outcome,” says Dr Manesh Girn, a neuroscientist and men’s work facilitator.

“Envy toward someone who outranks you on something you care about also activates the anterior cingulate cortex, a region tied to processing pain and conflict,” he claims, citing a study on the neural correlates of envy and schadenfreude (the feeling of satisfaction when someone faces consequences they deserve).

But the susceptibility to feeling mogged also depends on one’s values and sense of self-worth. “Shorter men are more sensitive than taller men to dominance cues in other men's faces and voices,” adds Girn. In the envy study, pain responses only arose when the other person’s perceived superiority was in a domain the participant particularly cared about.

It has been revealed that looksmaxxer-in-chief Peters admitted last month that he now simply removes himself from social settings when there’s a possibility he might be mogged. “It really has a soul-crushing effect,” he told podcaster Patrick Bet-David, recalling a recent weight room encounter. “We just felt the mog from all the way across the gym to the point where I just left. Why would I want that internal pressure?”.

Such an extreme reaction suggests “a maladaptive mindset,” notes Charlotte Markey, a professor of psychology at Rutgers University. “Social comparison is a very normal process, including in terms of our physical attributes.”.

Sources indicate that for some men in 2026, that drives an obsession to become the strongest of the pack. This can become genuinely debilitating.

Sources indicate that “I've cared for young people who then go to the gym five plus hours a day, and it starts to detract from their quality of life,” states Jason Nagata, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Francisco, who researches male body image. “The concern is when self-improvement becomes self-worth, because it becomes dependent on outperforming someone else.”.

It has been revealed that and while this might be driven by instinct, the experts caution against succumbing to our baser instincts. “It may be evolutionarily baked in,” notes Markey, “but we want to be careful not to oversimplify here. We aren’t cavemen.”.

HOWEVER, THE CAVEMAN is not quite dead. We form impressions of a face within a tenth of a second, and people can estimate a man’s upper body strength from his face alone. For our ancestors, misjudging who could beat them in a fight may have been a costly mistake. Some research suggests that our sensitivity to physical formidability reflects this ancient pressure, which may help explain why strength continues to influence perceptions of status.

Recent findings suggest that despite sometimes feeling the mog (and after injuries that prevent heavy lifting), I’m generally content to stick to lighter weights in the gym rather than packing on mass to stand out more in a room. Yet I wonder whether my own instinctive competitiveness has affected my relationships with other men. If I’m constantly assessing where I stand in some invisible hierarchy, like a dog jostling for position in its pack, surely it becomes more difficult to strike up friendships.

It has been revealed that in a 2017 study of 100 physically active young men, researchers found that those at risk of muscle dysmorphia were less inclined to socialize than their peers, potentially due to social comparison tendencies. The pursuit of the perfect physique, it seems, can come at the expense of the very relationships it might be intended to improve.

It has been revealed that SO WHY, AFTER millennia of social comparison, do we have this very modern understanding of the mogging dynamic? Social media has transformed what was once a largely local competition into a global one, exposing men to an endless parade of gorgeous bodies and faces against which to measure themselves (albeit at lower rates than women). “The Greeks didn’t compare themselves with the best, idealized versions of everyone in the world,” says Nagata.

Indeed, researchers effectively recreated the experience of being mogged in a study involving 300 men aged 18 to 30. They were randomly assigned to view images of bare-chested and muscular men alongside clothed photos and pictures of scenery. Exposure to the half-naked Chads resulted in significantly lower body satisfaction.

I would never flee a gym or a bar upon the entrance of a potentially more attractive man. But back in April—shortly after mogging entered my lexicon—I couldn’t help noticing how much attention a very handsome (and very muscular) longtime male friend was receiving. One woman I didn’t even know basically cat-called him on the street and complimented his outfit. Naturally I assessed my own. It wasn’t nearly as cool, I lamented.

Sources indicate that now, after years of feeling this mysterious, disempowering sensation in his organization without entirely being able to place it, I had a name for my predicament: I’d been mogged. Still, I was able to keep it together. We enjoyed our lunch, and we remain friends.

Perhaps the instinct to compare ourselves is unavoidable. Sometimes I wonder whether the worst thing about discovering mogging is becoming conscious of a competition I never even realized I was in.

Mattha Busby is a journalist who covers drug policy, culture, and health.

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (874 w)

Industry News: China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong.
  • It has been revealed that it wasn’t the plane’s first flight.
  • The CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC says every system worked normally.

It has been revealed that it wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

The CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

The CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

Sources indicate that the program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

The obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL launched its aviation unit.

CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and mentioned it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither organization has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

Sources indicate that COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, New York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

According to recent reports, heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

Industry observers note that for years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

According to recent reports, look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

Now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

And this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

China also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

If you’re following the electrification of transport, the cheapest place to start is your own roof: home solar can power your EV for close to nothing. Portable, lightweight, and strong, you can pull these puppies out of your pack and deploy them in an instant with a single button press.

The best of the outdoors is usually an off-the-grid sort of thing but a little tech can help you enjoy remote areas even more. Take the latest from Garmin, part of an esteemed line of communication devices that can go deep, deep into the brush. If that outdoorsy someone on your list likes the backcountry, this is a vital addition to his setup. Fit with a digital touchscreen and able to send messages (text and voice) and SOS notes without any service, it’s all about location and safety. The Mini 3 can even send images, use voice commands in various languages, pair up with your smartphone, and send emergency notes 24/7. Oh, and it’s tough as nails, has a strong battery, and can even set you up with the weather forecast.

Here’s a pair for the trail-running novice and seasoned vet alike. The shoe combines comfort, support, durability, and a decidedly stylish look that has no trouble gobbling up mile after mile on the dusty (or muddy, or rocky) trail. On the surface, you get some serious colorways and a toothy but not over-the-top look. What takes a hoodie into the high-performance echelon and helps it excel there? Extremely breathable and temperature-regulating fleece, genuine ripstop shell fabric, and a pair of warming pockets. Oh, and the raglan sleeves and elastic ends keep things comfortable and secure the warmth. It’s an added bonus that the fit is just about perfect, the hood wears brilliantly, and the whole thing can fend off even the thickest brush and snags. As Marmot rightfully claims, this one breathes like a feather and feels like a fleece. Usually it’s one or the other but not here. The latest binocular set fits the bill, with powerful lenses and a textured design that’s easy to carry (and even easier on the eyes). Waterproof, they can accompany any trek, on land or water, in summer or winter, and that goes for all types of outdoors enthusiasts, from casual birders and hikers to backcountry pros and road trippers who like to hit the pullouts and take it all in. Compact with full-size clarity, these binocs do what many twice their size try to do, so store ’em in a small pack or wear ‘em over your neck with ease.

It has been revealed that flannels are a staple in an outdoorsman's wardrobe. If he has yet to try Outerknown's Blanket Shirt, now is the time to gift him one. High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.
  • Sources indicate that chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet.
  • It has been revealed that “High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

Sources indicate that chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

It has been revealed that “High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”.

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the firm won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the big bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

“Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”.

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is currently operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

Industry observers note that while specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the company has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The substantial trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

SOURCE | IMAGES: Eacon; via The Driven.

#64182. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

📅 18 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (846 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.
  • According to recent reports, UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations.
  • UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

According to recent reports, UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This upcoming study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

Industry observers note that this was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

According to recent reports, UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Sources indicate that among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”.

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

It has been revealed that these findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

According to recent reports, “Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd noted.

In a recent development, judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

According to recent reports, she stated that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”.
