💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that most people have never seen a San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia).
  • In a recent development, however, conservationists recently scored a major win for the snakes.
  • According to recent reports, “Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work,” Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen) biologist Karine Tokatlian said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that most people have never seen a San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia). Native only to California’s San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties, the brilliantly colored reptile was one of the initial entries in the United States Fish and Wildlife Service’s first endangered species list in 1967. After nearly 60 more years of droughts, invasive species, disease, low genetic diversity, and poaching, researchers estimate only a few thousand San Francisco garter snakes still exist in the wild.

In a recent development, however, conservationists recently scored a major win for the snakes. For the first time, 62 of young serpents born at the San Francisco Zoo were released at specific sites across San Mateo County earlier this fall. The successful rewilding of dozens of the endangered snakes marks a huge moment for population rehabilitation efforts, and hopefully clears the way for similar releases in the future.

According to recent reports, “Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work,” Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen) biologist Karine Tokatlian said in a statement. “This first release is an vital step toward building healthy, resilient populations that can sustain themselves over the long term.”.

Although slender, the brightly colored San Francisco garter snake can grow anywhere from 18 to 55 inches long. Its eyes are larger than most of its fellow garter snakes, allowing it to keep active during daylight hours. With no fangs and only mildly toxic saliva, the snake is essentially harmless to humans, although its bites are fatal for prey like smaller reptiles and rodents.

The process of releasing young animals like these snakes that were reared in captivity is known as head-starting. It is an effective way to protect creatures during the most vulnerable stage of their lives. Head-starting the first batch of San Francisco garter snakes began in 2025, when conservationists collected multiple pregnant females from a healthy preserve in California’s Midpeninsula. Researchers later released the adult snakes back into their habitats after they gave birth, but kept the infants at the San Francisco Zoo. While there, zoologists conducted genetic testing on each snake to select the best possible locations for their eventual release. Conservationists deposited about one-third of them in the same area as their mothers, then placed the other two-thirds at locations particularly in need of greater genetic diversity pools for breeding.

As biologists continue to monitor the first generation of head-started snakes, another generation is already waiting for its time to shine. More than 130 garter snakes have been born at the San Francisco Zoo this year alone, with an eye to release them sometime in 2027.

Sources indicate that “This species is special in many ways, but unfortunately its critical status is not unique,” added Midpen wildlife ecologist Ariel Starr. “The success of this project and the associated research will not only benefit the San Francisco garter snake but will also hopefully inform the recovery of many imperiled reptile species.”.

  • Stuparich stated endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they mentioned the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich stated endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”.

According to recent reports, one possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers stated.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:.

Stuparich remarked she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel mentioned.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

Sources indicate that “These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Industry observers note that some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:.

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

Per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the upcoming production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla intends to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The tech giant says it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”.

It leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the newly introduced hall will be bigger than the original factory.

Industry observers note that the building isn’t fresh. Tesla laid out a proposal to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only said the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

Giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

So the fresh hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

Recent findings suggest that the EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

Tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

Sources indicate that rules can move in three years. The Commission has stated it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

Tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

Tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

The Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU remarked no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

Recent findings suggest that and the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

It has been revealed that that’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

This is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

Good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

Recent findings suggest that will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

Apple HomeView smart home hub review: Siri gets a swanky fresh house

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Industry observers note that apple’s $299 smart display has been sitting on my kitchen counter for about a week.
  • According to recent reports, the HomeView comes in two versions, and both cost $299 in the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

Industry observers note that apple’s $299 smart display has been sitting on my kitchen counter for about a week. It looks like a hybrid between an old-school iMac and a giant Apple Watch, but it’s a dedicated home for the recently revamped Siri. It’s an easy addition for anyone already committed to Apple gear. If your smart home runs on cameras, locks, or sensors that don’t work with Apple Home, though, you’ll want an upgrade blueprint before you buy one.

According to recent reports, the HomeView comes in two versions, and both cost $299 in the US. I tested the tabletop model, which mounts a 7-inch square touchscreen on a domed aluminum speaker base and includes a 30W power adapter and USB-C cable in the box. You can have it in any color you want, as long as it’s silver, starlight, rose pink, or space gray. The Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) drops the base and its extra speaker hardware, as well as the starlight/rose pink color options, and the panel costs more to put on a wall than its sticker price suggests. It requires a Schneider Home mount sold separately, and those start at $59.95. The cheapest USB-C mount also needs a power adapter of at least 20W, which you’ll have to supply yourself.

Recent findings suggest that the HomeView looks the way you’d expect an Apple product to look. Once you take off the protective coverings, the 2.1-pound, 6.82-inch tall device is pretty right out of the box. And it looks great between a breadbox and a butcher’s block, especially compared to an older smart screen that I’ve had there for years, which looks ancient next to it. A stainless steel hinge connects the screen to the base, so you can tilt the display toward wherever you’re standing. The screen stays firmly in place after you position it, even if you tap aggressively like I tend to. It doesn’t wobble or shake as you navigate on-screen menus.

Sources indicate that setting up the HomeView feels like setting up an iPhone or any other recent Apple device. It requires an iPhone running iOS 27.2 or later (or an iPad on iPadOS 27.2), so if your phone isn’t there yet, like mine wasn’t, you’ve got to stop and run the enhancement first. The HomeView played a soft, heavenly drone the whole time it waited, which is a much nicer way to sit through a software update than staring at a progress bar. Also, when you first boot things up, you might think you can immediately start asking for the kind of stuff you ask Siri on your iPhone, but you may have to go through a round or two of launching apps on the HomeView to give them permission to access your account even if your iPhone is with you.

Industry observers note that the HomeView’s Liquid Retina LED backlit screen has looked great in every lighting condition I’ve put it in. Apple rates the 1088-by-1088-pixel (220 ppi) display’s brightness between 0.3 and 500 nits, and that bottom end is what makes it work on a nightstand. In a dark kitchen, it reads as a soft glow instead of a floodlight.

Recent findings suggest that the multitouch True Tone touchscreen responds rapidly, and it kept registering taps even when my fingers were slightly wet (even though the device doesn’t have a specific water-resistance rating). That’s a real advantage for a screen that spends its life in a kitchen.

According to recent reports, the upcoming, more conversational Siri AI on the HomeView is a massive jump from the old Siri. The HomeView’s four-mic design ensures Siri can hear you from throughout the room and, when a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone is nearby, it can pull from personal data. If you ask about an upcoming concert, it can also check the calendar on your Apple account and tell whether you’re actually free to go.

It has been revealed that that personal access runs through the HomeView’s 12MP Center Stage camera. It can recognize up to six Home app-registered household members by face, and it only highlights someone’s personal information when it recognizes that person and their paired iPhone or iPad is on the same Wi-Fi network—with support for Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) with MIMO—and was recently unlocked. The HomeView’s A18 chip uses what Apple calls Secure Exclaves to process the camera and microphone feeds in a separate compartment, and Apple says neither the operating system nor Apple itself can access it. Those safeguards are reassuring on paper, though they aren’t something I could independently verify while testing a smart display in my kitchen.

That reliance on a nearby iPhone or iPad is also the source of the HomeView’s most frustrating quirk. With my phone on me, Siri sometimes can’t decide which device should answer. The first few times I tried to set a simple timer, it turned into a dance between the HomeView and my phone before one of them finally took the request. It takes a little getting used to.

Your iPhone also supplies a substantial share of the HomeView’s apps. There’s no App Store on the device. It ships with 15 built-in apps, including Safari, FaceTime, Music, and Home, and it pulls a handful of other Apple apps, like TV and News, from your phone. So, if you don’t mind some severe letterboxing, you can watch TV and movies on there. Supported third-party audio and video apps show up from a paired iPhone, too, through a system that works a lot like CarPlay. If a service you rely on doesn’t support it, there’s no way to install it on the HomeView directly.

The HomeView’s main job is running your smart home, and that’s where my experience was most mixed. It controls accessories you’ve added to Apple Home, which includes supported HomeKit and Matter devices. My Ring cameras don’t integrate with Apple Home natively, so they never appeared in the HomeView’s Home Camera face, which can otherwise show up to nine live feeds at once. It worked easily with my smart lighting and other natively compatible devices.

Check whether your current cameras, locks, sensors, and thermostat show up in Apple Home before you initiative to run the whole house from this screen. If they don’t, budget for HomeKit or Matter replacements that do (and Apple has a whole suite of new options developed alongside LG and Schneider Electric).

The actual smart hub interface that displays on screen is handy for keeping tabs on what’s going on in your home. It’s important to note that this thing looks like a thermostat when it’s on the wall, but it isn’t one. Maybe a future model with a built-in thermostat could free up some wall space.

The HomeView turned out to be a great cooking assistant. Once you open a recipe page on the web, either on your iPhone or in Safari on the HomeView, a Start Cooking button reformats it so you can follow the steps in real time while you work. Recipe pages vary wildly in how they’re formatted and coded, and I expected that mess to trip it up. It has worked without a problem every time I’ve used it so far.

It has been revealed that I made a fairly simple recipe for peanut butter noodles, and the instructions and timers were helpful and easy to use. More complicated recipes are more of a challenge, especially since you can’t really perform more than one step at a time, so don’t expect it to turn you into Gordon Ramsay overnight.

Recent findings suggest that as for the audio, the tabletop HomeView sounds full for its size. Its base holds a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators, almost like a subwoofer in miniature (but without the extension), and the display adds two custom full-range down-firing drivers of its own. I’d been using an older Google smart display before this, and the jump in sound quality is obvious.

According to recent reports, in separate tests, PopSci editor Tony Ware spent a couple of nights with his own HomeView and some of his favorite songs and came away with positive impressions. Compared to a HomePod mini, the beat hits more convincingly. While there’s not much room for excursion in the base, output manages to be surprisingly potent without sacrificing clarity. It won’t beat some recent whole-home audio-focused connected speakers (or Apple’s own full-sized 2nd-gen. HomePod, for that matter), but it’s plenty room-filling for such a compact, multipurpose enclosure. Whether you’re chopping carrots or choppin’ it up with friends, the HomeView is more than enough speaker for a smaller space.

What was more impressive was the airy, open presence of Dolby Atmos tracks from Apple Music, given the use of reflections and computational audio rather than an actual array of directional drivers. With accelerometers and Apple silicon adjusting the acoustic system’s EQ and output based on the screen’s tilt, the result is more incisive than immersive … how it will always be when you can’t surround yourself with speakers. Still, it projects clearly without sounding overly bright or edgy, which is good for podcasts to playlists.

There are occasional kinks, however. If you’re into spatial audio, the best way to ensure you’re getting the correct version of a track is to ask the HomeView to pull Apple Music directly from the cloud; sometimes the Dolby Atmos badge won’t pop up when you send a track from your phone over AirPlay, so you can’t be certain it’s not just stereo. Alternatively, you can hand off whatever is playing on your phone by bringing it close enough to the HomeView to get an AirDrop ripple animation and the album art to show up. Also, you might find yourself instinctively running your finger along the edge of the display looking for volume buttons, but there are no physical controls, which isn’t surprising from an aesthetic standpoint but still feels like a shortcoming.

According to recent reports, the Apple HomeView makes the most sense on a nightstand, on the wall next to your thermostat, or in the kitchen. Its Photos face turns it into a digital picture frame, which keeps it from looking like a giant Apple Watch stuck to your wall or sitting on your table (though the clock faces are cute and colorful).

Recent findings suggest that if your home already runs on an iPhone and Apple Home accessories, HomeView slots right in and puts it all on one screen you’ll actually want to look at. If you’ve built your smart home around gear that doesn’t work with Apple Home, however, proposal to replace it before you make the jump.

BYD’s latest, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.

The Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China. In Europe and the UK, it’s sold as the Dolphin Surf, and in other overseas markets, it’s called the Dolphin Mini.

With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.

After launching the second-generation “Great” Seagull in China, a larger, more advanced version, BYD was expected to introduce it overseas as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

Apparently, that will not be the case. BYD will introduce the updated version overseas, but according to the Spanish media outlet TestCoches, it will replace the larger Dolphin hatch rather than the Dolphin Surf.

The second-generation model will offer BYD’s five-minute Flash Charging technology and Blade Batteries 2.0.

According to recent reports, in China, the newly introduced Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000). For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super Trade-In” promotion, bringing the starting price down to just 62,900 yuan ($9,500).

Sources indicate that the second-gen Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than its predecessor.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s newly introduced Seagull now offers room for five passengers, up from four in the outgoing version.

According to recent reports, instead of a front-wheel-drive powertrain, the newly introduced version switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from 55 kW (75 hp).

With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. To go from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

In a recent development, even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes just 3 minutes longer (12 minutes) to charge from 20% to 97%. However, Flash Charging is not included as standard on the two cheapest entry-level variants.

While the bigger dimensions and Flash Charging were the biggest updates, BYD also added a few premium extras.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

Inside, BYD revamped the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The fresh setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a redesigned two-spoke steering wheel and center console with smart storage, plus added physical buttons.

All versions are equipped with BYD’s DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system.

The optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance is available. It includes a roof-mounted LiDAR to provide ADAS features such as City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

Sources indicate that in China, BYD offers the new Seagull EV with two Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh. The former provides a CLTC range of up to 320 km (199 miles), while the latter provides up to 420 km (261 miles).

The current Dolphin Surf measures 3,990 mm in length, and the Dolphin is 4,290 mm long. Selling the updated version as the Dolphin makes more sense, given how much closer in size it is.

BYD will continue selling the Dolphin Surf in Spain and throughout Europe, with the updated model now featuring five seats and a few other key improvements.

In Europe, BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at about €22,990 ($25,000), and the larger Dolphin is priced from around €33,990 ($37,500).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that in 2003, the basin was excavated as an extension of the Khor Kalba mangrove trees.
  • “Our results show just how critical coastal wetlands can be to young green turtles,” Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for one group of young sea turtles, a protected wetland in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) proved a perfect oasis. A team tracking nine juvenile green turtles (Chelonia mydas) found they were spending over 80 percent of their time in the Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area, a human-made lagoon on the UAE’s Gulf of Oman coast. Large numbers of turtles are also found in this basin built beyond the salt-tolerant trees and shrubs along the coast. A study published today in the journal Aquatic Conservation details the findings.

Recent findings suggest that in 2003, the basin was excavated as an extension of the Khor Kalba mangrove trees. The resulting Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area has been recognized as a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention and as a Key Biodiversity Area since 2013.

“Our results show just how critical coastal wetlands can be to young green turtles,” Dr. Owen Exeter, a study co-author and marine conservation ecologist from the University of Exeter, said in a statement. “The fact these turtles are using the artificial basin appears to be a happy accident, and an example of how wildlife can find a way in a world increasingly shaped by humans. However, without the natural mangroves connecting to this system, it’s unlikely that this would have occurred.

According to the team, the floor of the basin is covered with algae, which likely means the turtles have enough food. A few sharks are making their way to this habitat.

The turtles are now also showing “strong reliance” in the man-made basin, with five times higher odds of being found there than in surrounding habitats.

While this spot can be a refuge, the natural mangrove channels also play a critical role in connecting the juvenile turtles (those with a shell less than 23 inches across) to the sea. These channels allow them to move with the tides and show the importance of protecting the entire ecosystem, not just parts of it.

“The government of Sharjah currently protects most of this area from building development, fishing and boating—preserving the last mangrove ecosystem on UAE’s east coast,” Exeter said. “Coastal wetlands are tropical nature hotspots, providing essential nursery and foraging habitats for species including sea turtles. Wetlands are among the most threatened ecosystems globally, so we urgently need to understand how key species use both modified and protected wetlands.”.

In a recent development, while these findings are positive for the turtles living in the protected area, their life cycle depends on nesting beaches. Many of these beaches have already been lost to coastal development, and fishing, vessel traffic, and pollution affect the other nearby areas.

One of the turtles swam over 430 miles south to central Oman, highlighting the need for conservation management of these mobile species once they are old enough to leave critical wetland sites.

“Overall, our findings show that coastal wetlands, including engineered ones, can provide valuable habitat for juvenile turtles, provided they are designed for ecological connectivity and subsequent human pressures and threats are minimised,” concluded study co-author Brendan Whittington-Jones from the Sharjah Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA) who led the study.

Industry News: ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.
  • Industry observers note that the research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people.
  • While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Industry observers note that the research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they revealed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Industry observers note that despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is right now no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”.

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” noted Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”.

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

Recent findings suggest that ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

According to recent reports, “I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed.

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” noted Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:.

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:.

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more.
  • In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects.
  • Sources indicate that jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Life in a busy newsroom went on.

Sources indicate that jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”.

In a recent development, the fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a substantial topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Industry observers note that many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

Sources indicate that the line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Industry observers note that since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She states her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”.

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

According to recent reports, but despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”.

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” remarked Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

It has been revealed that “There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she states. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”.

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”.

Sources indicate that it’s vital to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

According to recent reports, stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger.
  • Recent findings suggest that tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and states it has the car’s event data recorder and video.
  • on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators states Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.

Recent findings suggest that tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and states it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

At 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.

Recent findings suggest that the SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

It has been revealed that FHP noted the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.

According to recent reports, under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

Industry observers note that it identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph, a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.

According to recent reports, this record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it notes Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.

Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

According to recent reports, how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.

Industry observers note that most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.

It has been revealed that so Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.

According to recent reports, autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s important to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?

Industry observers note that there’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.

Recent findings suggest that this is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.

The same release set a fresh record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.

This is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.

In a recent development, tesla certainly benefits by keeping the information hidden. Most are willing to look past these things and not be suspicious, but ultimately the question is why hide. something if you dont have something to hide.

In a recent development, we’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.

If FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.

Recent findings suggest that we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland. How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?

#64116. Tech Report: Smartwatch blood pressure monitoring was okay. AI is making it better.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1009 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Smartwatch blood pressure monitoring was okay. AI is making it better.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When the United States Food and Drug Administration cleared the Apple Watch’s Hypertension Notification Feature last year, some saw it as a turning point in the fight against one of the leading causes of cardiac disease.
  • While that sounds great, the reality of smartwatch hypertension tools is more nuanced.
  • That context is worth keeping in mind when considering new research from scientists at Google and a clinical partner from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School recently published in the journal Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the United States Food and Drug Administration cleared the Apple Watch’s Hypertension Notification Feature last year, some saw it as a turning point in the fight against one of the leading causes of cardiac disease. Rather than booking a doctor’s appointment and strapping a bulging cuff around one’s arm, consumers could instead receive passive hypertension alerts from the watch’s optical sensors to track blood flow patterns. Watch wearers who were previously unaware that they had signs of this ever-common “silent killer” would receive an alert advising them to seek out a clinician. Early intervention could mean a better chance at beginning life-saving interventions.

While that sounds great, the reality of smartwatch hypertension tools is more nuanced. Apple’s own validation data showed that their feature would miss around 59 percent of people with undiagnosed high blood pressure. Newer United States population level research from the University of Utah and the University of Pennsylvania went a step further, and warned that the absence of an alert could give wearers a false sense of security, potentially making them less likely to go get a proper cuff screening. The feature, in other words, isn’t necessarily harmful, but it also isn’t a medical silver bullet.

That context is worth keeping in mind when considering new research from scientists at Google and a clinical partner from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School recently published in the journal Nature. The team claims they created a new AI system that pairs with a consumer smartwatch to passively detect signs of high blood pressure, “with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed blood pressure devices.”.

Recent findings suggest that the latest system draws on two sensors already found in many consumer smartwatches: an optical pulse sensor (which tracks changes in blood volume at the wrist) and an accelerometer. An AI algorithm then analyzes several days of  readings, factors in the wearer’s height, and then calculates the probability that they have hypertension.

Sources indicate that google’s system builds on Apple’s approach by adding in the watch’s accelerometer to the mix, which can pick up the faint wrist vibrations of each heartbeat. The results look promising. In initial screenings, the combined system caught more cases of high blood pressure than a standard office cuff reading, though it still missed about a third of cases. And while the researchers involved still advise against using the tool as a substitute for seeing a doctor, it’s potentially another step forward in attempts to use common wearable tech to catch underlying signs of disease earlier.

“By gently prompting at-risk individuals to step into a clinic for formal assessment, this technology holds the potential to significantly close the global awareness gap and catch hypertension before it causes permanent cardiovascular damage,” Google researchers note in a blog post.

Heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the U.S. , claiming more than  900,000 lives in 2023 alone. Chronic high blood pressure (referred to as hypertension medically) is one of the key early risk factors. Around half of all Americans likely have it, but an estimated four in ten people don’t know they have it, partly because it often does not present with any clear symptoms. And while hypertension is treatable when caught early, many simply don’t see a doctor often enough to be screened regularly. That combination of an invisible condition and spotty screening makes the issue an attractive target for always-on smartwatch sensors.

It has been revealed that the sensors on commercial smartwatches can pick up useful data, but those signals still need to be interpreted by an AI model. In this case, Google claims it trained its system on nearly 500,000 hours of sensor data collected from 2,109 people. The optical sensor captures the shapes of each pulse wave at the wrist, while the accelerometer indicates signs of the subtle physical vibrations that occur at the wrist when blood is ejected from the heart into the aorta. Both of those signal data are cut into 5-second PPG and ACC waveforms. The AI converts those signal snippets into numerical summaries, which Google refers to as an “embedding.”.

Over time, the AI model was able to pore over those different numerical values and determine which types of pulses are likely associated with hypertension. By analyzing data collected from one wearer to the next, the AI sees numerical patterns that distinguish one person’s signals from another. But simply relying on a measurement from one point in time risks introducing what the researcher calls “environmental noise” that can skew results. To account for all that noise, they aggregated the sensors’ data over multiple days of use to establish a wearer’s persistent state. That data then gets fed into a logistic regression classifier, which comes out with a score corresponding to a person’s likelihood of having hypertension.

Recent findings suggest that the team tested their system on 196 participants over seven days of real-world monitoring, checking their results against 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, which they refer to as the “gold standard” in the field. The AI smartwatch system ultimately detected hypertension with a sensitivity of 65.8 percent. That means 65.8 percent of people who were proven to have hypertension were accurately identified by their AI system. That’s far from perfect, but it was still higher than the 55.3 percent caught by initial office cuff readings in the study.

“Taken together, the results show that our system can detect hypertension with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed BP devices in the existing clinical framework,” Google notes.

Like Apple before it, Google and the other medical researchers involved in this story were quick to stress that these findings, noteworthy as they may sound, shouldn’t lead people to think of this system as a complete replacement for clinical blood pressure monitoring .Going to see actual human doctors isn’t going away anytime soon, but this system, if widely accessible, could help nudge more people towards getting checked out.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honda’s automatic engine start-stop feature is under newly introduced federal scrutiny, after the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration received hundreds of complaints that engines failed to restart automatically from a complete stop at a traffic light on certain models, prompting the agency to commence an investigation.

It has been revealed that the federal probe, announced on Friday, November 13, includes 1.03 million units of the 2024-2026 Honda Passport, Odyssey, Pilot, and Ridgeline. The inquiry also includes 2024-2026 Acura MDX units. NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation received 701 complaints related to the Auto Start/Stop feature.

In a recent development, “To help improve fuel efficiency, the Auto Start/Stop system will automatically shut off the engine when a vehicle comes to a complete stop. The engine is intended to automatically restart when a driver releases the brake pedal. However, the complaints allege that the engines are failing to restart once they have been shut off by this system,” the investigation announcement reads.

While automatic start-stop systems were created to improve fuel economy, Honda seems to be having a recurring issue with the feature. Federal safety regulators previously opened a probe into Honda’s automatic start-stop system in 2025. That investigation included 2.2 million late-model Honda Pilot, Odyssey, Passport, and Ridgeline models, as well as Acura MDX and TLX units. However, the new investigation includes 2026 model-year units. Inquiry documents allege that the two issue populations have different root causes and respond differently to repairs.

There have been no injuries related to this issue, according to the feds. EPA boss Lee Zeldin remarked the agency was investigating improvements or eliminating the technology last year; whether it sticks around in the long run, however, an engineering analysis of the stop-start system should bring Honda and NHTSA together to identify an effective solution to this recurring problem soon.

In a recent development, soft daylight and tactile finishes lend Sarah Elliott’s interiors an easy, unhurried feeling. Her photographs for Upstate invite a closer look at country living, while her work with Elizabeth Roberts, Nune, and others brings that intimacy to many homes.

A bedroom on the Upper East Side of New York, designed by The Interiors Concierge and styled by Pablo Olguin.

Whether a space is minimalist or maximalist, Claire Esparros is able to distill its essence by amplifying the serenity or vibrancy of her photos. Framing spatial sequences and highlighting vignettes are among her strengths.

A landing in Kacey Musgraves’s Nashville home.

Sources indicate that lelanie Foster’s portraits of Serena Williams, Kacey Musgraves, and Misty Copeland for AD make the home as compelling as the person. For designers seeking photographs that introduce the inhabitants as well as the interiors, her portfolio merits a look.

A bedroom designed by Mieke ten Have and photographed by Frank Frances in New York’s Hudson Valley.

Trained in art practice at the School of Visual Arts, photographer Frank Frances has contributed his versatile eye to AD, British Vogue, West Elm, and others. His photography, which expands beyond interiors into beauty, food, and fashion, has appeared in exhibitions at galleries across the world, including Sasha Wolf Gallery, the Studio Museum of Harlem, and Werkstadt Graz.

Kirsten Francis captures a collectors’ trove.

In a recent development, an NYC–based lifestyle photographer specializing in interiors and portraits, Kirsten Francis has shot sun-drenched spaces by a roster of designers including Ashley Darryl, Alyssa Kapito, and Emily C. Butler.

A family room in Park City, Utah, designed by Wendy Labrum Interiors.

In a recent development, if Athena Calderone’s coffee table book Live Beautiful has earned a permanent spot on your coffee table, you’re already acquainted with Nicole Franzen’s photography. The New York talent’s portfolio also spans hospitality and cookbooks, giving homebodies and hosts alike something to savor.

Inside a private home on the Amalfi Coast.

It has been revealed that the skill with which Patrick Fraser is able to portray history and character in his images is captivating. Born in the UK and recently relocated to Connecticut from the West Coast, he often takes inspiration from objects, landscapes, and people that have been forgotten or ignored.

A modern retreat nestled in nature.

This Brooklyn-based creative has brought an expert eye to shoots in countless stylish homes, restaurants like Altro Paradiso, and the studios of talents like Trueing and Christian Siriano.

The sunlit living room of a townhouse in Upcoming York City’s West Village.

Inside celeb stylist Kate Young’s upstate New York home.

A vignette from Elsa Perretti’s home in Spain.

Adrianna Glaviano finds visual wit in the smallest arrangements, such as jewelry on striped straws, or personal effects gathered around a sink. Her still-life sensibility offers designers a way to make the objects within a room part of its story. An Upstate Latest York couple painstakingly restored this geometric 1970s hideaway.

Golden hour appears to be Nick Glimenakis’s choice time to shoot, when he’s able to capture the warm light, long shadows, and exaggerated contrasts that up the drama in his imagery.

An indoor-outdoor space designed by Mike Moser Studio.

Recent findings suggest that residential design and hospitality meet in Christian Harder’s portfolio, which includes work with Jake Arnold, Ash, and AvroKO. A marble bathroom in a Finger Lakes estate designed by Jeremiah Brent.

Ethan Herrington’s career began in commercial still-life photography, and places and things get equal billing in his portfolio—welcome news for those who obsess over both the room and its contents. Based in Cold Spring, New York, he has worked with Billy Cotton, Commune, and Studio Dorion.

A sunken living room oozes cool in this airy abode.

Studio Valle de Valle transformed a historic home in Toronto.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that many of the Muppets are pretty easy to pin down, species-wise.
  • Industry observers note that well, in a new episode of Popular Science’s Ask Us Anything podcast, we asked three biologists to break down exactly what Gonzo is.
  • Ask Us Anything answers your most outlandish, mind-burning questions—from the everyday things you’ve always wondered to the bizarre things you never thought to ask.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that many of the Muppets are pretty easy to pin down, species-wise. Kermit is a frog. Fozzie is a bear. Miss Piggy is, obviously, a feisty piggy. But Gonzo—with his blue-ish fur, bulging eyes, tuft of purple feathers, and long, curved nose that looks a little like a beak—is something of an enigma. The writers of the Muppets have avoided the question of what Gonzo is for years.

Industry observers note that well, in a new episode of Popular Science’s Ask Us Anything podcast, we asked three biologists to break down exactly what Gonzo is. We also talk to Muppets legend and Gonzo performer Dave Goelz to get his take.

Ask Us Anything answers your most outlandish, mind-burning questions—from the everyday things you’ve always wondered to the bizarre things you never thought to ask. So, yes, there’s a reason candy tastes different now and no, you don’t need to worry about Yellowstone’s supervolcano blowing up anytime soon. If you have a question for us, send us a note. Nothing is too silly or simple.

This episode is based on the Popular Science article “What kind of animal is Gonzo?”.

Listen and follow Ask Us Anything on your favorite podcast platform:.

Spotify | Apple Podcasts | YouTube | Or wherever you get your podcasts.

Sarah Durn: Picture some of the most recognizable characters from The Muppets. Maybe you’re thinking of Kermit the Frog, or Miss Piggy, or Fozzie Bear. But today, we’re talking about a Muppet who’s a little harder to describe: Gonzo. You know the one. He’s got bluish fur, major bulging eyes, a tuft of purple feathers on his head, and a long curved nose that looks a little like a beak.

You might know him as The Great Gonzo, the fearless daredevil, performance artist, and stunt Muppet who eats tires, catches cannonballs bare-handed, and courts his beloved Camilla, who is a chicken. So yeah, Gonzo is a pretty unusual guy. But here’s something you might never have stopped to think about. What exactly is Gonzo?

Is he a bird, a lizard, an alien? All of the above? For decades, Muppets cast and creators have mostly dodged the question when asked, but here at Popular Science, we wanted a more scientific answer. So we asked three biologists to take a closer look at Gonzo’s anatomy and tell us what kind of creature he might be.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk once promised the fully autonomous, steering-wheel- and pedal-free Tesla Cybercab would arrive before the year 2027, and start at less than $30,000. Prominent tech influencer Marques Brownlee promised back in 2024 to shave his head if Tesla delivered on that cost and timeline. It appears that the automaker, very technically, has done so, as Tesla declared on X on Friday evening that “select customers” can now purchase a Cybercab through an early-access, limited-release program.

Cybercab pricing starts at $29,990, a price that includes the first month of the autonomy subscription required to operate the vehicle; every subsequent month, however, users will need to pay $299 for that subscription. Customers can reserve a Cybercab with a non-refundable $1000 deposit. Deliveries in Austin, Texas will begin in December 2026.

According to recent reports, but, as the saying goes, there’s a catch. The first one here is that owners can only operate the Tesla Cybercab in areas where it has been approved for use. According to Tesla’s website, that presently includes major cities in two states: Austin, San Antonio, Dallas-Fort Worth, and Houston in Texas, and Tampa Bay, Orlando, and Miami in Florida. Tesla’s website lists Las Vegas, Phoenix, and Jacksonville as “coming soon.”.

Another restriction is that Tesla is not selling the Cybercab to fleet operators—the most obvious customer—just yet. Customers in this initial batch may purchase one Cybercab, and only for personal use. However, Tesla does have an interest form that potential fleet operators can fill out on its website.

According to recent reports, the Cybercab and autonomous driving in general represent potentially game-changing technology—a major reason automakers and major tech companies have invested heavily and worked on it for more than a decade. In theory, Tesla and third-party operators could offer incredibly low ride-sharing prices, with no driver who needs to be compensated with humane wages. Prices would be low enough not just to undercut rideshare providers such as Uber and Lyft, but potentially to undermine personal vehicle ownership itself.

But achieving that Tesla-driven utopia may be a far-off prospect. To change the game, the technology must work. As Jeremy Clarkson and others have noted, Tesla’s Cybercab ride-sharing service still has several kinks to work out. Broad regulatory approval remains a relatively distant prospect. And even if the technology works and meets safety standards, customers still have to buy in.

Breaking: Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

📅 24 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.
  • The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.
  • Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

In a recent development, “Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”.

According to recent reports, “Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a strategy that works for them.”.

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

According to recent reports, “Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”.

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

According to recent reports, “This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”.

In a recent development, sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, mentioned that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:.

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”.

Sources indicate that “There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”.

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”.
